Charles Ives, born in 1874 and died in 1954, was an American modernist composer who is now recognized as one of the first American composers of international significance. Believing that a professional musician could be forced to compromise their artistic freedom, Ives pursued a highly successful career in the insurance business, composing in his spare time. His music was decades ahead of its time, incorporating radical experiments with polytonality, polyrhythms, quarter tones, and tone clusters, often overlaid with nostalgic quotations of American hymns, folk songs, and marching bands.

The Unanswered Question, written in 1908, is a short, philosophical chamber work in which a trumpet plays a phrase representing the Perennial Question of Existence over a slow string background representing the Silences of the Druids, while a woodwind quartet tries and fails to answer the question, becoming increasingly chaotic. Concord Sonata, his Piano Sonata No. 2 from 1915, is a monumental work dedicated to transcendentalist writers associated with Concord, Massachusetts including Emerson, Hawthorne, the Alcotts, and Thoreau. It famously requires the pianist to use a fourteen point seventy-five inch wooden block to play massive tone clusters. Three Places in New England from 1914 is a brilliant orchestral suite depicting regional historic sites, and its second movement, Putnam's Camp, famously recreates the acoustic experience of two marching bands playing completely different tunes as they march past each other. His Symphony No. 4, completed in 1916, is a colossal, multi-layered work that is so rhythmically complex it often requires two conductors to perform, serving as a summation of his philosophical and musical ideals. Central Park in the Dark from 1906 is an atmospheric chamber piece that portrays a quiet night in New York City interrupted by distant streetcars, ragtime music, and rowdy crowds before settling back into a quiet string drone.

Ives and Myrick was the highly successful insurance agency he co-founded in New York. He pioneered the modern concept of estate planning and wrote a widely read pamphlet on insurance sales before his health forced him to retire. He was a foundational figure of American classical music who pioneered experimental techniques long before European composers did. Aaron Copland championed Ives's music, helping to bring his long-ignored works to the attention of the mainstream classical public in the nineteen thirties and forties.
